body.text: Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyānam (Phv)
body.translated_text: <s>Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna</s> (Explanation of the Heart of Dependent Arising)

body.text: ācārya nāgārjunakṛtam
body.translated_text: Composed by <s>Ācārya Nāgārjuna</s>.

body.text: iha kaścit śuśrūṣamāṇaḥ śramaṇaḥ śravaṇa dhāraṇohāpohaśaktisampannaḥ śiṣya ācāryasya pāda [mūla] māgamya tathāgataśāsanamārabhya evaṃ pṛṣṭavān - bhagavan atra
body.translated_text: Here, a certain student — a renunciant endowed with the capacity for listening, retaining, and critical analysis, wishing to learn — approached the feet of the <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) and, with reference to the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, asked thus: 'Venerable one, regarding

body.text:
dvādaśa ye 'ṅgaviśeṣā muninoddiṣṭāḥ pratītyasambhūtāḥ /
kva teṣāṃ saṅgraha iti śrotumicchāmi / iti /
body.translated_text:
the twelve distinctive links which the Sage declared to arise dependently —
where are they subsumed?' I wish to hear.

body.text: tasya teṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ tattvavubhutsāmavetya ācārya idamuktavān

children.translated_text: They are subsumed, as they truly are, in three categories: <s>kleśa</s> (defilements), <s>karma</s> (action), and <s>duḥkha</s> (suffering).

body.translated_text: Having understood his desire to know the true nature of those <s>dharmas</s>, the <s>ācārya</s> spoke thus:

body.text: tatra daśa ca dvau ca dvādaśa / aṅgānyeva viśeṣā aṅgaviśeṣāḥ / rathāṅgavadaṅgabhāva uktaḥ / kāyavāṅamanomaunānmuniḥ / tena muninoddiṣṭāḥ kathitāḥ prakāśitā iti paryāyāḥ / te ca na prakṛtiniyatipuruṣaparādhīnakarmaīśvarakālasvabhāvayathecchāprajāpatiyadṛcchādikāraṇaprasūtāḥ / kiṃ tarhi pratītyasambhūtāḥ / te dvādaśāṅgaviśeṣāḥ kleśakarmaduḥkhā anyonyaṃ pratītya naḍakalāpayogena triṣu yathāvat saṃkṣiptāḥ / yathāvaditi aśeṣeṇetyarthaḥ || 1 ||
body.translated_text: Here, ten and two make twelve. The links themselves are the distinctive [members] — hence 'distinctive links.' The nature of their being links is stated to be like the parts of a wheel. The Sage (<s>Muni</s>) is one who is silent in body, speech, and mind. 'Declared by that Sage' means spoken, taught, and illuminated — these are synonyms. And they do not arise from nature, fate, a supreme person, dependence on another, action [of a prior agent], God, time, inherent nature, wish, <s>Prajāpati</s>, chance, or any such cause. What then? They arise dependently. Those twelve distinctive links — [classified as] defilements, actions, and sufferings — are subsumed, as they truly are, in three [categories], depending upon one another in the manner of a bundle of reeds. 'As they truly are' means without remainder.

body.text: pṛcchati / ke punaste kleśāḥ / kiṃ karma / kiṃ duḥkham yeṣu ime pratyayaviśeṣāḥ saṅgrahaṃ gacchanti / āha -
body.translated_text: The student asks: 'What then are those defilements? What is action? What is suffering? — in which these distinctive conditions are subsumed.' The teacher replies:

body.text: ādyāṣṭamanavamāḥ syuḥ kleśāḥ / dvādaśāṅgaviśeṣāṇāṃ[madhye] ādyā avidyā, aṣṭamī tṛṣṇā, navamamupādānam ime trayaḥ kleśasaṅgṛhītāḥ pratyavagantavyāḥ / kiṃ karma /
body.translated_text: The first, eighth, and ninth are defilements. Among the twelve distinctive links, the first is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the eighth is <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving), and the ninth is <s>upādāna</s> (clinging) — these three should be understood as subsumed under defilements. What is action?

body.text: karma dvitīyadaśamau ca / saṃskāro dvitīyaḥ bhavo daśamaḥ /[imā] dvau dharmau karmasaṅgṛhītau veditavyau /
body.translated_text: Action is the second and the tenth. <s>Saṃskāra</s> (volitional formations) is the second; <s>bhava</s> (becoming) is the tenth. These two <s>dharmas</s> should be understood as subsumed under action.

body.text: śeṣāḥ sapta ca duḥkham karmakleśasaṅgṛhītānā [maṅga] viśeṣāṇāṃ ye śeṣā[aṅga] viśeṣāḥ sapta ca te duḥkha[saṅgṛhītā] veditavyāḥ / tadyathā vijñānaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ sparśo vedanā jātijarāmaraṇam / ca śabdaḥ priyaviyogāpriyasaṃyogeṣṭavighātaduḥkhāni sañcinoti /
body.translated_text: The remaining seven are suffering. Of the distinctive links subsumed under action and defilements, the remaining distinctive links — seven in number — should be understood as subsumed under suffering. Namely: <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form), <s>ṣaḍāyatana</s> (the six sense-bases), <s>sparśa</s> (contact), <s>vedanā</s> (feeling), <s>jāti</s> (birth), and <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (old age and death). The word 'and' (ca) accumulates the sufferings of separation from the beloved, union with the unloved, and the frustration of desires.

body.text: trisaṅgrahā dvādaśa tu dharmāḥ || 2 ||
body.translated_text: Thus the twelve <s>dharmas</s> are subsumed in three [categories].

body.text: atra ete dvādaśa dharmāḥ karmakleśaduḥkhā[khyā] veditavyāḥ /[anyūnā] dhikajñapanārthastu śabdaḥ / etāvanta eveme sūtrāntanirdiṣṭā nātaḥ paramastīti parigaṇitam || 2 ||
body.translated_text: Here, these twelve <s>dharmas</s> should be understood as [classified under] the names of action, defilements, and suffering. The word 'tu' (but) is for the purpose of indicating neither fewer nor more. These alone, just this many, are set forth in the <s>sūtras</s> — it has been enumerated that there is nothing beyond this.

body.text: pṛcchati / kleśakarmaduḥkhānā[meṣāṃ] kutaḥ kimutpadyata iti vyākhyātuṃ prārthaye / āha -
body.translated_text: The student asks: 'I request you to explain — from what does each of these defilements, actions, and sufferings arise?' The teacher replies:

body.text: tribhyā bhavati dvandvam kleśākhyebhyastribhyaḥ karmākhyaṃ dvandvamutpadyate / dvandvātprabhavanti sapta duḥkhākhyāḥ pūrvanirdiṣṭāḥ / saptabhyaḥ / traya udbhavanti kleśākhyāḥ / tebhyastribhyaḥ kleśebhyaśca dvandvamutpadyate / bhūyastadeva tu bhramati bhavacakram || 3 ||
body.translated_text: From the three [defilements] arises the pair [of actions]. From the three called defilements, the pair called action arises. From the pair arise the seven called sufferings, as previously stated. From the seven arise the three called defilements. And from those three defilements again the pair arises. And so this wheel of existence revolves again and again.

body.text: bhavāḥ kāmarūpārūpyasaṃśabditāḥ / [te ca] anavasthānāccakrabhūtāḥ / teṣu pṛthagjano loka eva paribhramati / tuśabdaśca aniyatajñāpanārthaḥ / yathā cakramanupūrvyāṃ paribhramati / na tathā triṣu bhaveṣūtpattiḥ / [kiṃ tarhi] niyamo nāstīti jñāpayati || 3 ||
body.translated_text: The existences are designated as the desire realm, form realm, and formless realm. Since they have no fixed ground, they are like a wheel. In these, the ordinary worldling alone revolves. The word 'tu' (but) is for the purpose of indicating indeterminacy. Just as a wheel revolves in regular succession, birth in the three realms of existence does not follow such [regular order] — it indicates that there is no fixed rule.

body.text: pṛcchati / atha sarvadeheśvaraḥ sattvākhyaḥ kartā / teṣu tasya kriyā kīdṛśī / āha -
body.translated_text: The student asks: 'Now, is there a lord of all bodies, a doer called a "being"? What kind of action does he perform in these [existences]?' The teacher replies:

body.text: hetuphalañca hi jagat prajñaptiṃ vihāya anyo nāsti kaścidiha sattvaḥ / paramārthataḥ kalpitaḥ / kalpitaśca nāsti / kalpitamātraviṣaye(kāma) iṣṭadravyaṃ sat na yujyate /
body.translated_text: For the world is only cause and effect — setting aside conventional designation, there is no being whatsoever here. From the standpoint of ultimate truth, [the being] is merely imagined. And what is imagined does not exist. In the domain of mere imagination, a desired real object is not logically tenable.

body.text: pṛcchati / yadyevam, tarhi asmāllokāt kaḥ paralokaṃ saṅkrāmati / āha / asmāllokātparalokaṃ sūkṣmo 'ṇurapi na saṅkrāmati / atha ca śūnyebhya eva śūnyā dharmāḥ prabhavanti dharmebhyaḥ || 4 ||
body.translated_text: The student asks: 'If this is so, then who transmigrates from this world to the next?' The teacher replies: From this world to the next, not even a subtle atom transmigrates. And yet, from empty [dharmas] alone, empty <s>dharmas</s> arise from [other] <s>dharmas</s>.

body.text: ātmātmīyarahitebhyo dharmebhyaḥ kleśakarmākhyebhyaḥ pañcahetubhyaḥ śūnyebhya ātmātmīyarahitā duḥkhatayā kathitāḥ phalakalpitāḥ śūnyāḥ sapta dharmāḥ prabhavantītyarthaḥ / tadyathā ātmātmīyarahitāste nānyonyaṃ punarātmīyāḥ / atha ca svabhāvato 'nātmadharmabhyaḥ svabhāvato 'nātmadharmāḥ prabhavanti / evamavagantavyamiti jñāpitam || 4 ||
body.translated_text: The meaning is this: from the five causes (<s>hetu</s>) called affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) and action (<s>karma</s>) — <s>dharmas</s> that are devoid of self and what belongs to self (<s>ātman</s> and <s>ātmīya</s>), and that are empty (<s>śūnya</s>) — the seven <s>dharmas</s>, which are devoid of self and what belongs to self, which are designated as suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), imagined as effects, and empty, come into being. To explain: those [causes] are devoid of self and what belongs to self, nor again are they mutually [each other's] property. And yet from <s>dharmas</s> that are by nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) non-self, <s>dharmas</s> that are by nature non-self arise. Thus it is to be understood — this is what is made known. || 4 ||

body.text: atra svabhāvato 'nātmadharmebhya eva svabhāvato 'nātmadharmāḥ prabhavanti ityatra ko dṛṣṭāntaḥ / atrocyate -
body.translated_text: Here [it is asked]: as for [the statement] that from <s>dharmas</s> that are by their very nature non-self, <s>dharmas</s> that are by their very nature non-self arise — what is the example here? To this it is said:

body.text: svādhyāyadīpamudrādarpaṇaghoṣārkakāntabījāmlaiḥ / ebhyo dṛṣṭāntebhyaḥ kalpitebhyo 'pi svabhāvato 'nātmanaśca paralokasiddhirveditavyā / tadyathā - gurumukhāduścaritā yadi śiṣyaṃ saṅkrāmanti / guruṇoccaritāstadvirāhatā api syuriti na saṅkrāmanti / śiṣyeṇa proktamapi nānyato 'sti / ahetubhūtatvāt / yathā gurumukhāduccaritāḥ tathā maraṇāṃśikacittamapi / śāśvata[ākhya] doṣaḥ syāt paraloke na saṅkramaḥ / paraloko 'pi nānyato bhavati / ahetudoṣasattvāt / yathā guruṇoccāritahetoḥ śiṣyeṇo[ccāritaḥ] sa eva anyo vā iti na nirṇetuṃ śakyate / tathā maraṇacittaṃ pratītya aupapattyaṃśikaṃ cittamapi tadeva tāto 'nyadvā iti na vaktuṃ śakyate / tathā / yathā pradīpātpradīpaḥ, mukhāt darpaṇe pratibimbamutpadyate / mudrātaḥ pratimudrotpadyate / arkakāntādagniḥ bījādaṅkuraphalāni amlarasāt rasavatpunaḥ, śabdātpratiśrutkaścotpadyate / te ca ta eva vā tato 'nye vā iti na jñātuṃ śakyate / tathā -
body.translated_text: By recitation, lamp, seal, mirror, sound, sun-crystal (<s>arkakānta</s>), seed, and the sour taste — by these examples, though they too are [merely] imagined, the establishment of the next world (<s>paraloka</s>) from what is by nature non-self should be understood. To explain: if [the recited words] from the teacher's mouth were to transfer to the student, then, having been uttered by the teacher, they would be devoid of him; thus they do not transfer. Yet what is recited by the student is also not from elsewhere, because of being without a cause (<s>ahetu</s>). Just as [the recitation] uttered from the teacher's mouth, so too is the mind at the moment of death. [If it transferred,] there would be the fault [called] eternalism (<s>śāśvata</s>); [yet] in the next world there is no transmigration (<s>saṅkrama</s>). The next world too does not come about from elsewhere, because of the fault of being without a cause. Just as it cannot be determined whether what is uttered by the student, by reason of what was uttered from the teacher, is that very same [utterance] or another — so too, depending on the mind at death, it cannot be said whether the mind of the moment of rebirth (<s>aupapattyaṃśika</s>) is that very same one or another than that. Likewise: just as from a lamp [another] lamp [is lit], from a face a reflection arises in a mirror, from a seal a counter-seal is produced, from a sun-crystal fire [arises], from a seed sprouts and fruits, from a sour taste again a juicy [thing], and from a sound an echo is produced — and whether these are that very same or other than that cannot be known. Likewise:

body.text: skandhapratisandhirasaṅkramaśca vidvadbhiravadhāryau || 5 ||
body.translated_text: The connecting [from existence to existence] of the <s>skandhas</s>, and the absence of transmigration (<s>asaṅkrama</s>), are to be ascertained by the wise. || 5 ||

body.text: tatra pañcaskandhā rūpavedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñānākhyāḥ skandhāḥ / teṣāṃ pratisandhirniṣiddhaḥ / hetorhi phalamanyadutpadyate / asmāt lokātparalokaṃ na ko 'pi bhāvaḥ sūkṣmo 'pi saṅkrāmati / evaṃ cakrabhramaṇaṃ bhrāntivikalpavāsanayā samutpadyate / anta iti tu viparyayaḥ / tato nivartayitavyam / anityaduḥkhaśūnyānātmabhāvān na nityabhāvān vyāmuhyāt / asati vyāmohe na rāgaḥ / asati rāge na dveṣaḥ / asati dveṣe na karma karoti / asati karmaṇi nopādīyate bhāvaḥ / asatyupādāne na bhavamabhisaṃskaroti / asati bhave na jātiḥ / asatyāṃ jātau na kāyacittayorduḥkhaṃ bhaveta / evamacintyāt taddhetupañcakānnānyatphalamutpadyate / ayaṃ mokṣo veditavyaḥ / evaṃ śāśvatocchedādidurdṛṣṭayo 'panītā bhavanti || 5 ||
body.translated_text: Therein, the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) are the aggregates called form (<s>rūpa</s>), feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). Their [literal] reconnection (<s>pratisandhi</s>) is denied. For from a cause a different effect arises. From this world to the next world, no entity whatsoever, not even a subtle one, transmigrates. Thus the turning of the wheel [of existence] arises through the latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) of erroneous conceptualization (<s>bhrāntivikalpa</s>). 'There is an end' is, however, an inversion [of the truth]; one should turn away from it. One should not be deluded into [a notion of] permanent existence, [departing] from the [true] nature that is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. When there is no delusion (<s>vyāmoha</s>), there is no craving (<s>rāga</s>). When there is no craving, there is no aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>). When there is no aversion, one does not perform action (<s>karma</s>). When there is no action, [no further] existence is grasped (<s>upādāna</s>). When there is no grasping, one does not form [a new] becoming (<s>bhava</s>). When there is no becoming, there is no birth (<s>jāti</s>). When there is no birth, there would be no suffering of body and mind. Thus, from that inconceivable five-fold set of causes no effect other [than these] arises. This is to be understood as liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>). Thus the wrong views (<s>durdṛṣṭi</s>) of eternalism (<s>śāśvata</s>), annihilationism (<s>uccheda</s>), and the like are removed. || 5 ||

body.text: atra dvau ślokau bhavataḥ -
body.translated_text: Here there are two verses:

children.translated_text: Whoever imagines annihilation (<s>uccheda</s>) even in a most subtle thing,
being ignorant, he does not see the meaning of dependent arising (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>). || 6 ||
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything whatever to be added;
and having seen the real (<s>bhūta</s>) as it really is, the seer of the real is liberated. || 7 ||

body.text: ācārya nāgārjunakṛtaṃ pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyānaṃ samāptam /
body.translated_text: The <s>Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna</s> composed by the <s>Ācārya</s> <s>Nāgārjuna</s> is completed.
